tldr: The authors propose "Heave-Ho," a decentralized multi-humanoid control framework that coordinates via physical interactions through a shared object, speech, and local observations—without any network communication such as Wi-Fi. They demonstrate that a control policy trained on just two robots scales zero-shot, without any retraining, to teams of up to 10 robots, heterogeneous robots, and even human collaborators.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of Heave-Ho. At the high level, the leader's VLM selects the next skill from camera images and speaks it aloud. Each follower listens and synchronizes the start on a shared time schedule. At the low level, a residual policy trained via multi-agent reinforcement learning sits atop a frozen base whole-body control model, enabling cooperative control through the shared object without network communication.
overview:
Many tasks—such as carrying heavy furniture or transporting bulky items—exceed the power and stability limits of an individual humanoid. Solving them demands multi-robot collaboration. However, three major hurdles stand in the way: handling strong physical interactions through shared objects, visual long-horizon planning to navigate tight spaces, and strict execution synchronization where timing mismatches cause falls.

Existing centralized control approaches suffer from exploding state and action spaces as robot counts grow, and they remain vulnerable to communication delays and packet loss. To overcome this, this study focuses on a fully decentralized design: robots coordinate using only the forces transmitted through the shared object and their own onboard sensors (such as proprioception), without any direct inter-robot communication. To achieve this, the paper presents a hierarchical framework named "Heave-Ho."

At the low level, the authors build upon an existing single-humanoid whole-body tracking model and post-train a residual policy using multi-agent reinforcement learning to compensate for physical coupling. At the high level, a leader robot decides the next team action using a vision-language model (VLM). By combining speech (verbalization and microphone recognition) with a coarse time-slice grid, the team achieves millisecond-level start synchronization without relying on communication networks.

For validation, the authors constructed "HH-Bench," a benchmark comprising 12 collaborative tasks, and conducted extensive experiments in simulation and on real Unitree G1 hardware. While traditional baselines consistently failed, Heave-Ho achieved exceptionally high success rates. Remarkably, the exact same control policy trained on only two robots adapted seamlessly, without retraining, to teams of up to 10 robots, heterogeneous platforms, and human partners.
contributions: Built a decentralized low-level controller operating purely on local observations under object-mediated physical coupling, extending a single-humanoid whole-body tracking model through residual learning.
Proposed long-horizon planning with a vision-language model and a communication-free leader–follower synchronization mechanism using speech and a shared schedule grid.
Constructed and released "HH-Bench," a multi-humanoid benchmark spanning 12 challenging tasks involving teams of 2–10 robots, heterogeneous platforms, and human partners.

Demonstrated on real hardware and in simulation that a single policy trained with only two robots scales and generalizes without retraining to teams of up to 10 robots, heterogeneous humanoids (PM01), and human partners.

sections.heading: Why Is Collaborative Carrying So Difficult for Humanoids?
sections.summary: While single-humanoid control has advanced, collaborative execution is essential for transporting heavy objects. However, three intertwined challenges arise simultaneously: dynamic coupling through a shared object, visual long-horizon planning, and millisecond-level synchronization. This paper introduces "Heave-Ho," a novel framework that overcomes these hurdles in a fully decentralized, communication-free manner.
sections.details:
Single-humanoid locomotion and loco-manipulation have seen remarkable progress in recent years. Yet, when handling bulky furniture or heavy building materials in homes, construction sites, and warehouses, a single humanoid hits physical limits in strength, torque, and balance. Sharing the load across multiple robots is a natural solution.

However, achieving this involves three severe challenges. First is tightly coupled interaction. Because robots share the payload, a partner's footstep or minor hand vibration directly acts as a disturbance, disrupting balance and grip force. Second is vision-based long-horizon planning. The team must orchestrate a sequence of actions tailored to the surroundings—such as pivoting or shifting the payload vertically to squeeze through a narrow doorway. Third is synchronized execution. A slight mismatch in lifting or stepping timing can tilt and drop the load or pull a partner down.

Trying to solve this with centralized control—where a central computer gathers all sensor data and computes all motor commands—requires retraining policies whenever team size changes, and wireless dropouts or latencies prove fatal. Heave-Ho takes a strictly decentralized approach. It sends zero communication packets between robots, challenging the problem of scalable multi-robot collaboration where each agent relies solely on its own sensors and forces felt through the object.

sections.heading: From Single-Robot Whole-Body Control to Multi-Robot Teaming and Language Planning
sections.summary: This section reviews prior work across three domains: single-humanoid control, multi-robot coordination, and VLM-based task planning. Heave-Ho bridges these areas through multi-agent residual adaptation of a foundation model and network-free speech synchronization.
sections.details:
To contextualize this research, related work spans three major lines:

- Humanoid Whole-Body Control and Loco-manipulation:
Deep reinforcement learning and imitation learning have accelerated the acquisition of diverse whole-body skills. In particular, generalist whole-body models like SONIC have emerged, using large-scale motion tracking as a foundation for teleoperation and agile behaviors. However, the vast majority of existing studies focus on single robots, leaving contact-rich collaborative tasks physically linked through objects largely unexplored.

- Multi-Robot Cooperative Control:
Centralized policies, Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE) reinforcement learning, and diffusion-policy imitation have been explored for multi-arm and quadruped setups. Yet, in legged robots carrying shared payloads, most methods rely on pre-specified external contact points or network-based start synchronization. Autonomous long-horizon collaboration across multiple real humanoids remained unachieved.

- Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for Task Planning:
Hierarchical architectures using Large Language Models (LLMs) or VLMs as high-level planners to call low-level skills are taking root in robotics. Language-based planning exists for multi-robot teams as well, but typically requires continuous network communication to exchange text dialogues.

Heave-Ho differs fundamentally by building upon a frozen base tracking model, combining residual learning for physical coupling with speech-based leader–follower synchronization to enable fully decentralized collaboration free of network infrastructure.

sections.heading: How Heave-Ho Works: Residual Post-Training and Keeping in Sync by Voice
sections.summary: Heave-Ho consists of two levels: high-level VLM planning with speech synchronization, and low-level residual MARL control. Unifying skill endpoints to common hub poses allows seamless skill composition, while vocal announcements and a coarse time grid achieve perfect execution synchronization without communication.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Overall Architecture
Let $N$ be the number of robots in the team. The framework adopts a strict definition of decentralized execution: zero network communication packets are exchanged between robots during task execution. Robot $i$ observes only its proprioception (joint positions, velocities, IMU, etc.), short future reference motions, and nominal object specifications $\mathbf{c}=(L,W,H,m)$. Every few seconds, the high level selects a team skill, which the low level projects into each robot's local frame to drive all joints at 50 Hz.

### 3.2 Low Level: Multi-Agent Residual Post-Training
A key design decision here is the introduction of "Hub poses." Every skill (moving forward, backward, turning, lifting, lowering, etc.) begins and ends at one of two common rest poses: standing empty-handed ($S_0$) or standing upright holding the object ($S_1$). This allows arbitrary skills to be seamlessly composed in sequence.

To train the control policy, the single-agent base tracking model (SONIC) is kept completely frozen. Only a residual policy $\pi_\theta$ is trained, outputting delta joint targets or torques added to the base model. Learning whole-body locomotion and collaboration from scratch results in catastrophic sample inefficiency. Instead, the frozen model handles foundational locomotion, while the residual policy focuses entirely on counteracting disturbances and sharing loads through the object.

Training uses Multi-Agent PPO (MAPPO) under Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE). During training, the Critic evaluates value functions using global state information, but Actor parameters $\theta$ are strictly shared across all robots, taking only local observations at inference. Shared Actor weights keep parameter counts constant regardless of team size, which proves key to scalability. Furthermore, if any single robot fails, the entire team's episode terminates, imposing shared accountability that strongly incentivizes cooperative behavior.

### 3.3 High Level: VLM Planning and Speech-Based Synchronization
The high-level planner fine-tunes Qwen3-VL-2B with LoRA. From the leader's head camera image and task instruction text, it predicts the next team skill (walk forward, turn, unload, etc.) in a single token.

The standout highlight is speech-based synchronization. How do robots coordinate down to the millisecond without network packets? The system decouples "what to do" from "when to do it." The leader determines "what" and vocalizes it through a speaker, which followers detect via microphone speech recognition. For "when," the team adheres to a pre-shared coarse control-tick schedule (grid) on their internal clocks, triggering execution at the next upcoming slot. Because the grid slot is wider than acoustic propagation delays and minor speech-recognition jitters, all robots snap to the exact same time slot, launching skills simultaneously without network synchronization.

captions.F2: Overall system architecture. The high-level VLM inspects images and vocalizes team skills, while the low-level residual RL model runs decentralized at 50 Hz, absorbing physical coupling forces transmitted through the shared object.

sections.heading: The New "HH-Bench": 12 Demanding Collaborative Tasks
sections.summary: To evaluate contact-rich multi-humanoid collaboration, the authors created "HH-Bench." It covers 12 tasks featuring diverse physical constraints and long horizons, such as passing through narrow doors, unloading from trucks, climbing stairs, and carrying large tables.
sections.details:
Existing multi-agent benchmarks typically focus on drone formations or simple navigation, lacking benchmarks where humanoids experience strong dynamic coupling through shared objects. The authors introduce "HH-Bench" to fill this void.

HH-Bench includes 12 tasks designed for teams of 2 to 10+ robots, including mixed teams with humans and heterogeneous robots:
- Constrained-Environment Transport:
In the representative "Narrow door" task, robots cannot pass while holding the load crosswise. They must coordinate a 90-degree yaw rotation mid-flight so one walks forward while the other walks backward through the doorway. In the "L-shaped corridor," robots smoothly transition between forward walking and side-stepping.
- Diverse Contact Modes:
Beyond two-handed carrying, tasks cover shoulder-carrying a sedan-chair structure ("Palanquin"), shoulder-carrying construction steel ("Rebar"), pulling a "Fire hose," pushing heavy crates and millstones ("Box push / Millstone"), and a "Box handover" passing a box across different heights from a truck bed to a ground partner.
- Long-Horizon Skill Composition:
Because all skills connect via hub poses, multiple tasks can be chained together. For instance, two robots can carry an object up stairs, load it onto a cart, and then one robot can depart to hand another parcel to a third robot on a lower tier—benchmarking ultra-long-horizon composite tasks with dynamic team structures.

captions.F3: Visual observations from the leader's head camera alongside VLM-selected vocal commands over time, shown for real-world narrow door traversal (top) and simulated box handover (bottom).

sections.heading: Real-Robot Deployments and Zero-Shot Scaling: From 2 to 10 Robots, and to Humans
sections.summary: Experiments were conducted in simulation and on real Unitree G1 and PM01 robots. Heave-Ho achieved a 94.4% success rate in simulation, vastly outperforming baselines (which maxed out at 28.6%). Moreover, the exact policy trained on two robots generalized zero-shot to carrying large tables with up to 10 robots and collaborating with humans.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Experimental Setup
Real-world experiments primarily used Unitree G1 robots equipped with head-mounted ZED stereo cameras, alongside the EngineAI PM01 as a heterogeneous platform. Simulation training was conducted in Isaac Lab across 4,096 parallel environments.

### 5.2 Real-World Collaboration Results
Real G1 pairs completed narrow door traversal, L-shaped corridors, truck unloading, and precision placement using only speech synchronization without network communication. Across 100 real-world trials—including stair climbing and door traversal with a human partner—the system demonstrated high robustness with 92 successes. The hardest task was stair carrying (7/10 successes), where narrow tread depths left no margin for foot placement error.

### 5.3 High-Level Planner Comparisons
The fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-2B planner was compared against zero-shot GPT-6 (Astra) and CHORUS, a multi-robot VLA model. Across five long-horizon tasks (two real, three simulation), the proposed planner matched the success rate of human teleoperators. GPT-6 suffered frequent failures and had high inference latency (~6.46 s), whereas the proposed planner ran at just 52.5 ms on an RTX 4090—roughly 120 times faster. CHORUS failed on simultaneous carrying tasks because agents progressed asynchronously without execution synchronization (succeeding only partially on handovers).

### 5.4 Low-Level Control Ablations
Across all 12 simulation tasks, Heave-Ho averaged a 94.41% success rate. In contrast, frozen SONIC alone (without residual learning) reached only 0.01% (tracking locomotion but unable to exert collaborative force), training MARL from scratch without SONIC achieved 3.09% (locomotion collapsed), and training independent Actors per agent reached only 22.05%. These numbers quantitatively highlight the impact of residual post-training on a foundation model and parameter sharing.

### 5.5 Train with Two, Deploy with Many (Scalability)
One of the most striking findings: training took place entirely in an environment with just two identical G1 robots. Yet, thanks to the parameter-shared Actor and egocentric observation formulation, deploying this exact policy zero-shot allowed 4, 8, and 10 robots to cooperatively carry large tables in simulation without any retraining (Figure F7). On real hardware, a team of four G1s and a heterogeneous trio of G1 + PM01 + human carried large tables successfully in 37 out of 40 trials.

captions.F5: Real-world collaborative tasks. From narrow door traversal, L-shaped corridors, and truck unloading, to 4-robot G1 table carrying and heterogeneous teams with PM01 and humans, all tasks were completed without communication.
captions.F7: Simulation snapshots of the control policy trained on only two G1s deployed zero-shot, without retraining, to teams of 4, 8, and 10 robots. The parameter-shared design unlocks remarkable scalability.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Outlook
sections.summary: Heave-Ho establishes a decentralized, communication-free framework for multi-humanoid collaboration. Combining residual MARL, speech synchronization, and VLM planning enables strong zero-shot generalization from two-robot training to 10-robot teams and heterogeneous human-robot partnerships.
sections.details:
This paper presented "Heave-Ho," a fully decentralized, communication-free framework for tightly coupled, long-horizon multi-humanoid collaborative manipulation.

At the low level, combining a frozen whole-body tracking foundation model with residual reinforcement learning yields robust control that handles dynamic coupling through shared objects using only local observations. At the high level, a lightweight VLM provides consistent task planning, while a speech-based synchronization mechanism leveraging vocalization and shared schedule grids achieves millisecond-level coordination without data packets. Comprehensive evaluations on HH-Bench demonstrate baseline-surpassing performance, real-world physical robustness, and exceptional generalization that scales from two robots to 10 robots, heterogeneous platforms, and human partners without retraining.

sections.heading: Appendix: Real-World Implementation and Policy Distillation Pipeline
sections.summary: This section details hardware and training specifics, including the 3D-printed head camera mount for the real G1 and the Isaac Lab policy distillation pipeline leveraging privileged simulation data.
sections.details:
### Hardware Implementation
For the real Unitree G1, a custom 3D-printed two-piece mount (a forehead bridge and a rear-head cradle) was developed to securely fasten the ZED stereo camera (Figure F8). This ensures stable visual inputs to the VLM even under intense walking vibrations.

### Low-Level Policy Training Pipeline
Training was conducted in Isaac Lab with pairs of Unitree G1 humanoids. First, an asymmetric Teacher policy was trained with access to privileged simulation information (exact contact forces, full object dynamics). Its mean actions were then distilled into a Student policy relying only on local observations. Simultaneously, an adaptation module was trained to estimate privileged latent representations from local observations, followed by fine-tuning the Student with closed-loop MAPPO. This phased post-training pipeline significantly bridges the sim-to-real gap.

captions.F8: The ZED stereo camera mounted on the Unitree G1 head using custom 3D-printed parts (forehead bridge and rear cradle).

takeaways: Massive scalability via communication-free collaboration: By absorbing dynamic object coupling through local sensing and sharing Actor parameters, a controller trained on two robots generalizes zero-shot to 10 robots, heterogeneous platforms, and humans.

Effectiveness of residual post-training on foundation models: While training MARL from scratch collapses, placing collaborative residuals on top of a frozen single-agent tracking model drastically boosts sample efficiency and success rates.

Decoupling "what" and "when" for speech synchronization: Transmitting instructions via vocal tokens and snapping execution start times to a coarse shared schedule grid enables high-precision coordination without wireless infrastructure.
limitations: Sensitivity to acoustic conditions: Follower robots require quiet enough conditions and sufficient microphone sensitivity to capture the leader's speech clearly, carrying risks of misrecognition in extreme noise or over long distances.
VLM planner training overhead: Fine-tuning the high-level planner for new task domains requires collecting teleoperation demonstrations from human operators, demanding manual data collection effort.

Reliance on hub poses: Because all skills chain together through static hub poses, extending the framework to highly dynamic continuous motions—such as turning and traversing without stopping—remains constrained.
